p: `nums = [0,1,1,3]`, `maximumBit = 2` (mask `11`). The XOR of the whole array is `0^1^1^3 = 3`:

blocks.h: Why is the complement the best k?
p: `x ^ k` is largest when all `maximumBit` bits are 1. Since XOR with `k` flips exactly the bits where `k` has 1, choosing `k = x ^ mask` flips the zeros to ones and keeps the ones, giving `x ^ k = mask`, the maximum possible.

1829.takeaway: Maximum XOR per query: keep the XOR of the array, answer with its complement within maximumBit bits, then remove the last element by XOR-ing it out.

head: Code

blocks.h: Why is the best target the window's maximum?
p: Increments can only increase numbers, so the shared value must be at least the window's maximum; any larger target costs more. In sorted order the maximum is the right-end element, so the cost for the window is `x × size − sum`.
If a window `[l, r]` is too expensive for `x = nums[r]`, then for the next larger `nums[r+1]` the same left end is even more expensive. So the left pointer never moves back.

bullets: Space: O(1) extra besides the sort.

1838.takeaway: Most frequent element after k increments: sort, then slide a window whose cost to raise everything to the right end stays within k.

blocks.h: Why the maximal range for each minimum?
p: For a subarray, min-product = min × sum. If the minimum is fixed at `h`, extending the subarray to every neighbouring element that is ≥ `h` only increases the sum (all values are positive). So each element only needs its widest range, found with the monotonic stack: its previous-smaller to its next-smaller.

1856.takeaway: Subarray min-product: for each element as the minimum, use a monotonic stack to find its widest range and prefix sums for the range total.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Binary search on the row index, not on cells
2D peak finding in O(m log n)
Column of the maximum in the middle row
The row maximum is already ≥ its left and right neighbours, so only up/down remain to check
The cell below is bigger: a peak must exist in the lower rows
The cell below is not bigger: this row (or one above) contains a peak
The maximum of the final row is a peak

p: The search ends at row 1; the maximum of that row is at column 1, so the peak is at `[1, 1]` (value 30). Several answers can be valid; any peak is accepted.

blocks.h: Why is the row maximum a good probe?
p: The maximum of a row is automatically greater than its left and right neighbours. The only thing left to check is the cell above and below. If the cell below is larger, walking down from there keeps increasing until a peak (the grid is surrounded by −1, so the climb must end). That halves the rows each step.

bullets: Time: O(n log m) (a row scan per probe).

1901.takeaway: 2D peak: binary search on rows; probe the middle row's maximum and move toward the larger vertical neighbour.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Removal can expose NEW occurrences: removing `abc` from `aabcbc` leaves `abc` again
Do the last `m` kept characters spell `part`?
Check only the top of the stack after each push
Delete those characters in one step

p: `s = "daabcbaabcbc"`, `part = "abc"`:

blocks.h: Why a stack and not `while part in s: s = s.replace(part, '', 1)`?
p: Repeated `replace` rescans the whole string after each removal (O(n²) worst case). The stack removes an occurrence the moment it is completed and only re-checks the last `m` characters, so total work is about O(n · m).

blocks.h: Why the order of removal doesn't matter
p: The problem says to remove the LEFTMOST occurrence each time, and the stack removes occurrences in order of their right end. For this pattern the results coincide, since an occurrence completed first ends first and no removal can change an occurrence that lies fully to its left.

1910.takeaway: Remove all occurrences of a substring: push characters on a stack and delete the top m whenever they spell the pattern, which also catches occurrences exposed by earlier removals.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: BFS order of the nodes without a deque: appending to a list while looping over it visits the new items too
Number of nodes in the subtree of `u`, computed by processing `order` in reverse (children before parents)
Number of valid build orders: the count of linear extensions of a rooted forest (each room must come after its parent)
Modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem (MOD is prime), since we cannot divide under a modulus

p: `prevRoom = [-1,0,0,1,2]`: room 0 is the root with children 1 and 2; room 3 is under 1; room 4 is under 2.
5! = 120, and the product of subtree sizes is 5 · 2 · 2 · 1 · 1 = 20, so the count is 120 / 20 = 6. The code computes this with modular inverses and gets 6.

blocks.h: Why does n! divided by the subtree sizes count the orders?
p: Among all n! orderings of the rooms, a node must appear before everything in its subtree: its probability among random orders is 1/size (it must be first of its `size` subtree members). These events are independent across nodes in a tree, so the number of valid orders is n! × ∏ 1/size.

bullets: Time: O(n log MOD) for the modular inverses.

1916.takeaway: Count build orders of a tree: n! / ∏ subtree sizes, computed with modular inverses.

1922.takeaway: Count good numbers: positions are independent (5 choices on even indices, 4 on odd); use fast modular exponentiation.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum fee to be at city `v` having used EXACTLY `t` minutes
DP over (time, city): time is a dimension because the budget is on time
Start at city 0 at time 0, paying its fee
Arrive at `v` via edge `(u, v, w)`: you were at `u` at time `t − w`, and now pay `v`'s fee
Reaching the destination at ANY time within the limit

p: `maxTime = 10`, roads `0-1 (3)`, `1-2 (3)`, `0-2 (9)`, fees `[5,3,2]`. States reached (time → cost to be at city 0, 1, 2):
Going 0→1→2 takes 6 minutes and costs 5 + 3 + 2 = 10; the direct road takes 9 minutes and costs 5 + 2 = 7. Both fit in 10 minutes, so the answer is 7.

Dijkstra minimises ONE quantity. Here there are two: fee (to minimise) and time (a budget). The cheapest route may be slow and a fast route may be expensive, so time must be part of the state. DP over time handles the constraint exactly.

1928.takeaway: Min cost within a time limit: DP on (time used, city), relaxing every road at every time step; answer is the best over all times at the destination.
